# The prepared data by cohort {#sec-by-cohort}


The prepared curves of every NORMAL, BENIGN and CANCER sample from Nova 250 onwards, leaving out the 8 patients
excluded for a large left/right intensity imbalance (@sec-intensity). As in @fig-cohort (right), the samples are ordered by the height of the
water peak (the mean of the prepared curve over q = 20-22), highest at the top: fibrous/glandular samples at the top, fatty ones at the bottom.
We pick out the water-rich top 15% of all these samples (outlined) and compare the mean curves of each cohort's samples within it.

Going from NORMAL to BENIGN to CANCER we expect more fibrous/glandular tissue: more water, and a fat peak that is relatively smaller. The
preparation scales every curve so that its fat peak is 1, so a smaller fat peak shows up as a **higher water peak relative to the fat peak**.

::: {#cell-fig-by-cohort .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
kept = set(analysis_novas)
rows, names, labels = [], [], []
for label in COHORTS:
    label_novas, label_rows, label_names, *_ = ne.sample_view(by_label[label])
    keep = (label_novas >= NOVA_RANGE[0]) & (label_novas <= NOVA_RANGE[1]) & np.isin(label_novas, list(kept))
    rows.append(label_rows[keep])
    names += [n for n, ok in zip(label_names, keep) if ok]
    labels += [label] * int(keep.sum())
rows, labels = np.vstack(rows), np.array(labels)
with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    water = np.nanmean(rows[:, (q >= WATER[0]) & (q <= WATER[1])], axis=1)
order = np.argsort(-np.nan_to_num(water, nan=-np.inf), kind="stable")  # highest water peak at the top
rows, labels, names = rows[order], labels[order], [names[k] for k in order]
top = round(len(rows) * PART / 100)
top_novas = {label: {ne.row_nova(n) for n, l in zip(names[:top], labels[:top]) if l == label} for label in COHORTS}

def water_height(curve):
    return float(np.nanmean(curve[(q >= WATER[0]) & (q <= WATER[1])]))

with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    top_means = {label: (np.nanmean(rows[:top][labels[:top] == label], axis=0), int((labels[:top] == label).sum())) for label in COHORTS}
top_water = {label: water_height(mean) for label, (mean, _) in top_means.items()}

covered = np.flatnonzero(np.isfinite(rows).all(axis=0))
columns = slice(covered[0], covered[-1] + 1)
low, high = np.nanpercentile(rows[:, columns], (1, 99))
left, right = q[columns][[0, -1]]

plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7  # small text so both panels fit side by side on an A4 page
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.9))
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_box_aspect(1)
ax = axes[0]
ax.imshow(rows[:, columns], aspect="auto", cmap=cmap, vmin=low, vmax=high, interpolation="nearest",
          extent=(left, right, len(rows), 0))
ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((2, 0), right - 2, top, fill=False, edgecolor=TOP_COLOUR, lw=2.5, clip_on=False))
ax.text(right - 0.4, top / 2, f"top {PART}%", color="white", ha="right", va="center", fontweight="bold")
ax.axvline(14, color="white", ls="--", lw=0.8)
ax.set(title=f"{len(rows)} samples, {len({ne.row_nova(n) for n in names})} patients", xlabel="q (nm⁻¹)", xlim=(2, right), yticks=[])
ax.set_xticks([5, 10, 15, 20])
# an arrow up the left of the heatmap: low water peak (fatty) at the bottom, high (fibrous/glandular) at the top
ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.11, 0.9), xytext=(-0.11, 0.1), xycoords="axes fraction",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="black", lw=1.2), annotation_clip=False)
ax.text(-0.11, 0.07, "Fatty", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(-0.11, 0.93, "Fibrous/\nGlandular", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="bottom")

ax = axes[1]
for label, (mean, n) in top_means.items():
    ax.plot(q[columns], mean[columns], color=ne.STATUS_COLOURS[label], lw=1.6,
            label=f"{label}: {n} samples, water {top_water[label]:.2f}")
ax.axvline(14, color="black", ls="--", lw=0.8)
ax.set(title=f"Top {PART}% (water-rich), by cohort", xlabel="q (nm⁻¹)", ylabel="I(q), stretched (fat peak = 1)",
       xlim=(2, right), ylim=(-0.05, 1.3))
ax.set_xticks([5, 10, 15, 20])
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.09, right=0.98, bottom=0.1, top=0.93, wspace=0.35)
plt.show()
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}

:::


In the water-rich top 15%, the water peak relative to the fat peak is 0\.81 for NORMAL,
0\.96 for BENIGN and 1\.07 for CANCER.

## Does the water-rich top 15% tell patients apart? {#sec-top-selection}

If water-rich tissue carries the difference, comparing a patient's two breasts should work better for patients sampled in water-rich tissue. The
comparison is the one used throughout this report, set out in @sec-every-patient: each breast's Water:Fat (the ratio of the water and fat
Gaussian areas, @fig-water-fat) is worked out from the mean of **all** its scans, and we count the patients whose breast expected to have more
water (the CANCER breast in CANCER vs NORMAL, say) has the higher Water:Fat. Each patient counts once.

We repeat this for the patients with at least one sample in the top 15% of @fig-by-cohort. Each entry is the number of
patients whose first-named breast has the higher Water:Fat, out of the patients compared.


| Comparison | Every patient | Patients with a sample in the top 15% |
|---|---|---|
| CANCER vs NORMAL | 25/38 \(66%\)\, p = 0\.073 | **9/10 \(90%\)\, p = 0\.021** |
| BENIGN vs NORMAL | 22/52 \(42%\)\, p = 0\.33 | 6/11 \(55%\)\, p = 1 |
| CANCER vs BENIGN | 15/24 \(62%\)\, p = 0\.31 | 0/3 \(0%\)\, p = 0\.25 |

: The share of patients whose first-named breast has the higher Water:Fat, with the two-sided binomial p-value against 50%. Each breast is the mean of all its scans.

::: {.callout-important title="This is not a fair test"}
This selection is made after the measurements, by looking at the very signal we then analyse, so it is not a fair test on its own; a fair test
needs a rule that treats both breasts the same way, which is what the rule of @sec-on-the-fly does.
:::
